1: # Connected visual changes and local repair
2: 
3: Status: human-assisted reasoning hypothesis. A connected-field strategy has not been validated against local wording in a controlled generation test.
4: 
5: "Small" describes the requested extent of an edit. Its spatial reliability depends on the renderer's actual conditioning and controls. A video-plus-text request supplies no guaranteed pixel lock. At the same time, the present evidence does not justify a universal claim that these models cannot perform local edits.
6: 
7: Many apparently local properties are carried by several visible relationships. A glowing tabletop rim involves the contour, material, brightness gradient and nearby illumination; light on the legs can satisfy the color word while missing the intended part. A robe affects the silhouette, the chair's visible support and overlap with the book. Page light affects surface texture and the visibility of the open leaves.
8: 
9: In [[case-bernini-003-before-v3|the fantasy study]], preserving a fitted garment and placing restrained light along page margins describes a connected, legible scene. Both replay arms proposed related revisions. This supports identifying a concrete design conflict; their repair effectiveness remains unmeasured.
10: 
11: One strategy worth testing is to express a coherent target state for the interacting region: how its surfaces, contours and lighting fit together over the visible action. The region is a reasoning focus, not a mask. The task may also favor returning to an earlier input, keeping a satisfactory candidate, or attempting a genuinely local change when the renderer supports one.
12: 
13: The useful knowledge is which relationships carry the effect and what information the input supplies. A blanket instruction to regenerate everything would discard that distinction. [[media|Material and image formation]] supplies design context; [[wiki-scene-identity|identity and visibility]] helps interpret consequences; [[wiki-realization|changed realizations]] helps compare proposed interventions.

1: # Rewording and changed visual realization
2: 
3: Status: human-assisted mechanism hypothesis; revised prompts from the replay were not rendered.
4: 
5: A new visual realization changes a relevant relationship, image-forming process or conditioning input. It may remove a conflicting design, change how an effect is spatially carried, or use a candidate that already supplies useful visual structure. A new name for the same requested operation provides weaker evidence of such a change. Rephrasing can still alter a model's response; its value needs measurement.
6: 
7: In [[case-ditto-024-before-v3|Ditto's glitch replay]], the proposed mosaic followed a prompt that already requested image-bearing rectangles and displaced strips. Calling it a different realization left the key question unresolved: what would make scene content move within the blocks rather than produce new opaque overlays? In [[case-bernini-024-before-v3|Bernini's source restart]], transparent echoes and ribbons likewise overlapped earlier demands. These overlaps do not establish that another sample would fail; they limit the evidence for a specific repair mechanism.
8: 
9: By comparison, [[case-bernini-003-before-v3|removing the authored robe]] cancels a concrete occluding design choice. Keeping the fitted garment shape changes the requested relationship between clothing and chair visibility. Its projected benefit was not measured in this replay, but the proposed intervention is identifiable.
10: 
11: Bernini and Ditto receive the selected video and text under their configured renderer interfaces. Writing "composite transparent layers" describes a desired image; it does not invoke a layer compositor or spatial mask. Ground expectations in available controls and the input's visible information.
12: 
13: An explanation of a retry can identify the failed relationship and what the proposal changes using existing intent text. No additional reasoning form is required. When the proposal retains essentially the same visual operation, another attempt is a sampling or phrasing hypothesis; its uncertainty and cost should remain visible. A useful follow-up would compare the relevant prompts on the same input under paired settings.
14: 
15: Related: [[express-edits]], [[choose-editing-input]], [[combination|how visual methods interact]].

1: # Choose an editing input
2: 
3: [Experience map](README.md) · [Express an edit](express-edits.md) · [Inspect results](inspect-and-compare.md)
4: 
5: Version 1. Origin: initial common-sense guidance approved for use as a starting point. The route preferences below have not been established by a controlled multi-round comparison. Model-specific evidence can change them.
6: 
7: ## Build on a result that already does the useful work
8: 
9: When a candidate realizes most of the requested appearance and the remaining change is localized and describable, prefer trying the change on that candidate. Its achieved materials, layout and style become the input rather than something the generator must reproduce from a description. Select the candidate for this particular change; the latest video or the strongest overall candidate need not be the best editing input.
10: 
11: Treat locality as an intention to test. A whole-video editor may change other regions despite a local instruction. If relevant experience or the current result shows this behavior, consider another candidate or the original. A focused instruction is not a pixel mask or a guarantee that other regions stay fixed.
12: 
13: ## Recover a useful starting point when essential information is lost
14: 
15: If a candidate has substantially changed a key person, object, action or relationship, prefer an input that still contains the needed information, often the original. Repeated editing of a damaged representation can require the generator to invent missing structure. The original makes that structure available again, while the desired appearance must be generated anew.
16: 
17: A small remaining shape error does not automatically justify discarding a successful transformation. Inspect enough of the relevant area to judge the extent of the problem. When an older candidate already contains both the needed information and useful styling, it may be a better starting point than either the original or the latest result.
18: 
19: ## Start a substantially different direction from a suitable source
20: 
21: When changing the overall design direction, prefer the original if the existing result strongly embodies an incompatible earlier direction. Continue a candidate when the new idea intentionally builds on its appearance. A branch is simply another generated result with its own input and prompt; there is no obligation to settle on one direction early.
22: 
23: ## Use another sample when it can answer a real uncertainty
24: 
25: When the intended edit and instruction remain credible and one failure has no clear systematic explanation, another generation with the same input and prompt can help reveal whether the behavior repeats. Keep other settings comparable when that is the question. Such a sample consumes resources and does not itself repair an unclear instruction.
26: 
27: Repeated similar failures are a reason to reconsider the interpretation, expression, input or model capability. Merely replacing adjectives or adding stronger demands may repeat the same attempt without changing what the generator can do.
28: 
29: ## Revisit earlier results and stop when appropriate
30: 
31: If continued editing adds unrelated changes, return to a less damaged version and reconsider the next change. Preserve useful alternatives. Different candidates may be suitable for different next steps or final delivery; a single mandatory incumbent is unnecessary.
32: 
33: Continue when a further action has a plausible benefit for the actual request or can resolve consequential uncertainty. Finish when the available result is suitable, when further attempts have little expected value, or when resources end. A resource stop can leave an incomplete task; describe that outcome accurately.
34: 
35: ## Evidence available now
36: 
37: The [October 29 Bernini record](../model-experience/bernini-r.md) reports independent prompt conditions, not multi-round route comparisons. Its observed misplaced tabletop glow motivates inspecting the intended part, but does not establish that editing the generated video or restarting from the original is better. Subsequent route cases should retain input ancestry, prompts, settings, outcomes, evaluation conditions and counterexamples so these starting preferences can improve.

1: # Express an edit for its actual input
2: 
3: [Experience map](README.md) · [Design expression](../guides/design-expression.md) · [Bernini evidence](../model-experience/bernini-r.md)
4: 
5: Version 1. The input-aware recommendations are common-sense starting guidance. The Bernini observations below are scoped experimental evidence. No universal prompt length, sentence order or semantic-preservation recipe is established.
6: 
7: ## Write for what the generator receives
8: 
9: When generating from the original, describe the selected target coherently enough to realize the requested transformation. When continuing a candidate, describe the change relative to that actual candidate. A focused instruction is often a useful starting choice when most of the appearance is already achieved. A complete target description may be useful when several connected parts must change together. Choose the form for the task rather than a mandatory full/incremental label.
10: 
11: The renderer does not inherit the Planner's notes, earlier critique or unprovided reference videos. Words such as "fix that" or "restore the original" can leave the desired result unspecified. Describe the relevant wanted state when the renderer cannot see the comparison available to the Planner.
12: 
13: ## Keep detail relevant to the current design
14: 
15: A precise local request generally benefits from expression centered on the requested change and its dependencies. An open style request can benefit from developing a specific interpretation through visible relationships. Length alone does not determine which task needs more design work. Avoid expanding a narrow request simply to demonstrate creativity or use every available piece of knowledge.
16: 
17: Bind an important attribute to the intended object or part. A luminous tabletop rim and illuminated table supports are distinct targets. Explain a material relationship when it defines the design: pencil showing through transparent pigment conveys more than an unrelated list of materials. A clearer instruction still needs output inspection.
18: 
19: If a prompt is too large for the actual renderer, return to the design and choose which information matters. The runtime reports known limits; it does not silently cut text or append a universal template.
20: 
21: ## What the Bernini probe actually supports
22: 
23: On the recorded 041 task, the short storybook request remained largely photographic, while versions with concrete pencil-and-watercolor features produced a clear illustration. This supports trying a visible elaboration of the selected medium for that model and task. The short etching request on 027 also worked, so elaboration is not uniformly necessary. Length and information content changed together.
24: 
25: The table-tennis outputs put blue glow mainly on lower supports despite a requested edge effect. Clearer part binding is a plausible wording improvement, not a demonstrated repair. Additional preservation clauses had inconsistent effects. Do not treat stronger wording as proven protection of structure or motion.
26: 
27: The [complete record](../model-experience/bernini-r.md) retains model revision, configuration, actual submitted text, outputs and reviews. The [design-application guide](../guides/design-expression.md) connects source reading to authored proposals; its new wording is identified as untested.
